title: Financial Transaction Surveillance: The Money Trail as Map
body:
## Overview
In GLMZ, the near-complete digitization of financial transactions — driven by the dominance of corporate token economies, the decline of physical currency, and the integration of payment infrastructure with civic identity systems — has made financial transaction data one of the most comprehensive and legally accessible surveillance records available to both government and corporate actors. Every purchase, transfer, debt service payment, and internal token exchange generates a timestamped, identity-linked record that is retained by the issuing financial institution, the Civic Financial Registry, and — for transactions occurring within corponation zones — the relevant corponation treasury system. Physical currency has not been abolished, but it circulates almost exclusively in the Outer Ring's informal economy and is treated by enforcement agencies as presumptive evidence of intent to evade financial monitoring.

## Analytical Capabilities
Financial transaction records, when analyzed at scale, produce behavioral profiles of extraordinary granularity. Purchase timing and category patterns reveal sleep schedules, dietary habits, social relationships, health conditions (through pharmacy and medical service purchases), and political sympathies (through donation records and attendance at fee-bearing civic events). Transaction graph analysis — mapping the network of financial relationships between individuals — is a standard law enforcement technique for identifying organizational structures in cases involving organized crime, labor organizing, and suspected corponation espionage. The ORACLE-7 predictive analytics platform incorporates financial anomaly detection as one of its primary feature inputs, flagging deviations from established spending baselines as behavioral risk signals.

## Access Tiers and Legal Constraints
Law enforcement access to financial records is governed by the Civic Financial Privacy Act of 2187, which requires a judicial proxy authorization for records older than 30 days and permits real-time transaction monitoring under a broader Financial Surveillance Order, which is issued with minimal judicial scrutiny for investigations involving financial crimes, terrorism, or infrastructure interference. Corponations have access to financial records generated within their token systems without any external authorization requirement. Employers routinely analyze employee spending patterns within corporate retail and service environments as part of CLMP operations. Credit rating agencies maintain parallel financial behavioral databases that are sold commercially and have no meaningful legal access restrictions.

## Informal Economy and Resistance
The Outer Ring's informal economy — operating in physical currency, barter, and the gray-market cryptocurrency networks that survive despite periodic enforcement crackdowns — represents a significant portion of lower-tier economic activity precisely because it is financially invisible. Estimates of the informal economy's size range from 12% to 31% of total Outer Ring GDP, with the variance reflecting the fundamental difficulty of measuring what is designed not to be measured. Participation in the informal economy is not itself illegal, but the absence of a financial record for a period longer than 14 days triggers an automatic compliance review under Civic Identity Maintenance statutes — a provision that effectively penalizes financial invisibility and pushes lower-tier residents toward monitored systems regardless of their preference.
